title: Boethius in prison
hook: condemned and waiting, he writes the Consolation of Philosophy, where Lady Philosophy comes to his cell

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's picture of love: the one who loves, the one who is loved, and the love between them. Your line was love in three. Where did you see all three at once? Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

A man sits in confinement, writing sad poems. Not long ago he was a powerful official at the king's court. Now, as he tells it in his own book, he has been condemned, his good name is gone, and he's waiting. The Muses of poetry stand around his bed, feeding him lines of grief. Then a woman appears above his head. Her robe is old and torn, as if rough hands had ripped pieces away. She looks at the Muses and sends them packing. She sits on the edge of his bed and wipes his eyes with a fold of her dress. He knows her. She's Philosophy. This is Boethius in prison.

The book is called the Consolation of Philosophy, and it's a conversation between a broken man and the wisdom he had studied all his life. Philosophy doesn't start with comfort. She starts with diagnosis. You've forgotten who you are, she tells him. Then, in the second book, she brings out an image: Fortune's wheel. In one passage Philosophy speaks in Fortune's own voice. I turn a wheel, Fortune says. I bring the low up and the high down. Climb on if you like, but don't call it unfair when the wheel brings you down again. That's the rule of the game you agreed to play. Change isn't Fortune betraying you. Change is what Fortune is. So Philosophy asks Boethius to look at what he's lost. Money, office, applause. Were they ever really his? The things that can be taken away were only on loan. What can't be taken is the good itself, and Philosophy leads him, step by step, toward God as that highest good, the still center the wheel turns around. Here's the surprise. Boethius was a Christian who wrote on the Trinity, yet this book never names Christ. The help comes from reason, from Philosophy. Christian readers have still treasured it, hearing echoes of scripture in it. Hannah's song in the first book of Samuel says: "The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up." And Job, stripped of everything, says: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
screen: `WHAT CAN BE TAKEN WAS ON LOAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: console yourself with wisdom. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that's gone badly lately, a loss, a no, a door that closed. Let it be as heavy as it is. Now let a wise friend sit on the edge of your bed, the way Philosophy sat with Boethius. Ask what they would point to. What did this take that was only on loan? What's still yours? If you pray, you can bring both answers to God. The bell holds the time.
Boethius in prison. A condemned man who wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, where wisdom visits his cell and turns him from Fortune's wheel to the good that can't be taken.
Your line: the wheel turns. Today, when something goes up or down for you, say it under your breath, and ask what part of you the wheel can't touch. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Christian readers have turned to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy in times of loss, and the image of Fortune's wheel appears in Christian art, poetry and preaching.

fork.setup: you're Philosophy. you find your old student in a cell, writing sad poems with the Muses. what do you do first?
options: join in and help him write sadder poems.
send the Muses away and tell him he's forgotten who he is.
fork.reveal: she drives off the Muses, wipes his eyes, and starts with a diagnosis: he has forgotten who he is.

original.note: Latin: the wheel of Fortune, the image at the heart of book two of the Consolation.

trapdoor: what you thought: the wheel of fortune is a game show.
what it means: in Boethius's book, Fortune turns a wheel by nature, so what she gives was only ever on loan.
what a scholar hears: a Christian thinker consoled by Philosophy, not scripture, led by reason toward God as the highest good.
